title: Terry Winters: Vitalized Geometry
summary: Terry Winters: Vitalized Geometry presents 44 prints and works on paper by the American artist Terry Winters, who draws inspiration from mathematical systems and structures of the natural world. Celebrating two groups of gifts to the Menil and organized in close consultation with the artist, the career-spanning presentation explores the importance of printmaking to Winters’s practice and its dialogue with other forms of making. Each medium is an instrument. Almost in a musical sense, meant to be played; and each affects the developing imagery. How they look, how they feel, and what they mean is conditioned by the materials and procedures. Media is used to embody an image actual size, as vitalized geometry—hopefully with a sense of life. Terry Winters: Vitalized Geometry is curated by Sophie Asakura, Curatorial Associate, The Menil Collection. Two gifts to the museum will be displayed in an exhibition tracing nearly four decades of the artist's works

title: Fragility
summary: This display highlights paper itself—and its incongruous and variable characteristics—as an artistic material. Included are works that present a range of processes, as well as paper sculptures and found papers that imbue a finished work with an additional sense of history and place. Among the artists featured in the exhibition, Lee Krasner relentlessly critiqued her own art, often destroying drawings only to reconstitute them as abstract collages. Ann Hamilton also brought papers together in surprising ways. In her collaborative work poche, 2014, she stitched soft wool between sheets of handmade paper to reflect on the pocket as both storage and protection for the body. Zarina grieved the loss of her husband and her native India by painstakingly puncturing paper with a needle to form intricate compositions. Featured artists include Lynda Benglis, James Lee Byars, Gene Charlton, N. Dash, Robert Fried, Ann Hamilton (in collaboration with Dieu Donné), Mona Hatoum, Jim Hodges, Hong Hong, Čestmír Kafka, Lee Krasner, Tony Lewis, Sol LeWitt, Brice Marden, Robert Rauschenberg, Mimmo Rotella, Susan Rothenberg, Amy Sillman, Adriena Šimotová, Kiki Smith, Leon Polk Smith, John Sparagana, Richard Tuttle, and Zarina. Fragility is curated by Kelly Montana, Associate Curator, Menil Drawing Institute.

title: Wall Drawing Series: Jitish Kallat
summary: Jitish Kallat's site-specific wall drawing grows out of his sustained engagement with Project A119, a partly declassified 1958 plan by the United States Air Force to detonate a nuclear bomb on the moon. In Wall Drawing / Redux: A119, Kallat introduces enlarged images derived from his previous work Accordion of Drawings / Project A119 / Early Intuitions, 2025, in which delicate watercolor graphics evoke an unrealized episode of ambition, secrecy, and violence during the Cold War. The process of creating the work began with the printing of all 190 declassified pages of the document onto the Menil Drawing Institute's 36-foot wall, forming a dense field of text and graphics. The wall was then sheathed in laminated glass that echoes an architectural detail of the building itself. Magnified and transferred across the glass, the watercolor images overlap with the archival text. The glass is treated with PDLC film, a material, a material whose transparency can be regulated electrically. Across nine panels, a slow gradient moves through changing states, with each cycle lasting roughly 500 seconds; the approximate time it takes sunlight to travel from the Sun to the Moon and return to us as moonlight. As transparency shifts, images emerge, dissolve, and reappear, while the documents move in and out of legibility. The changing surface moves between redaction and reappearance. Kallat describes this as “a constant shift between the condition of wall and that of window.” These ruptures also become apertures into the Project A119 document beneath. Wall Drawing Series: Jitish Kallat is curated by Edouard Kopp, John R. Eckel, Jr. Foundation Chief Curator, Menil Drawing Institute. The series began in 2018 as part of the Institute’s commitment to seeking new approaches to the form and language of drawing. Past participants include Marc Bauer, Mel Bochner, Roni Horn, Marcia Kure, Gladys Nilsson, Ronny Quevedo, and Jorinde Voigt.

title: How to Make an Exhibition: The Story of Jermayne MacAgy
summary: This exhibition honors the impact and legacy of the late San Francisco- and Houston-based curator, art historian, and museum director Jermayne MacAgy (1914–1964), who was renowned for her dynamic and groundbreaking installations and innovative approach to curating. MacAgy was among a vanguard of professionals in the 20th century who transformed the art museum into a site of conversation and learning. Working closely with Menil Collection founders John and Dominique de Menil from the mid-1950s until her death a decade later, she deeply impacted the future museum. She encouraged the couple to build a teaching collection and publicly exhibit their art using display techniques that encouraged curiosity and engagement. Dominique de Menil once recalled that MacAgy’s installations created an “atmospheric miracle, which set the work of art in such a light that it would shine and talk to anyone who would care to listen.” How to Make an Exhibition: The Story of Jermayne MacAgy is curated by Michelle White, Senior Curator. Weiner and Leslie Field; and the City of Houston through Houston Arts Alliance.

title: D’MBA: Beauty, Desire, and Collecting an African Mask
summary: D’MBA: Beauty, Desire, and Collecting an African Mask is a focused research and exhibition project examining the large wood headdresses commonly referred to as d’mba, nimba, or yamban among the Baga, Nalu, and neighboring peoples living in Guinea, West Africa. Worn and performed by men for ceremonies and public celebrations that mark significant moments in the cycle of life, the d’mba headdress is the sculptural embodiment of female personhood, sustenance (agricultural and maternal), physical beauty, and generational continuity. During the mid-20th century, at the height of the international market for African art in the United States, the d’mba became one of the objects most coveted by collectors. D’MBA unites for the first time a significant group of headdresses on loan from several art museums in the United States, including Art Institute of Chicago, Baltimore Museum of Art, Davis Museum at Wellesley College, National Museum of African Art, and Yale University Art Gallery. The exhibition of these headdresses, which were acquired during the late 1950s by prominent collectors in the United States, occasions a rare opportunity to pursue a thorough study of these icons of African art at the intersections of mask-making, colonial art education, independence-era cultural politics and religious iconoclasm in Guinea, and the international art market. Concurrently, in the museum’s galleries of African art, the Menil will present Baga Nimba, 2020. The seven-foot tall, gold leaf sculpture by Houston-based Nigerian artist Adeniyi Olagunju Haastrup epitomizes the Pan-African and Diasporic significance of the d’mba headdress from Guinea and its reinvention as a global art form. D’MBA: Beauty, Desire, and Collecting an African Mask is curated by Paul R. Davis, Curator of Collections, The Menil Collection.

title: Sedona Surreal: Max Ernst and Dorothea Tanning in the American Southwest
summary: In 1946, Max Ernst and Dorothea Tanning left New York City, then the center of the Euro-American art world, for Sedona, Arizona. Over the next ten years, they created some of the most significant works of their careers in this small desert town. Sedona Surreal will reunite the paintings, sculptures, and other artworks that they made there, exploring the construction of artistic modernism far from a large urban center. It will be the first museum exhibition devoted to Ernst and Tanning’s pivotal time in the Southwest. Why do artists remain in cities? Must they chum with collectors, attend openings, witness name-droppings in upper east and west side pastures...in order to make good pictures, good objects, and good anything? No, we will do it the other way. Sedona Surreal: Max Ernst and Dorothea Tanning in the American Southwest is curated by Natalie Dupêcher, Associate Curator of Modern Art, The Menil Collection.

title: John Akomfrah: The Hour Of The Dog
summary: John Akomfrah: The Hour Of The Dog is an immersive, six-channel video installation by the British artist Sir John Akomfrah. The work, co-commissioned by the Menil Collection and the Baltimore Museum of Art (BMA), explores the history of youth-led Civil Rights–era activism in the American South from 1954 to 1963, and how the participants fought for racial equity through nonviolent marches, protests, boycotts, and voter registration efforts. Activism is not confined to what happens in the streets; it’s bound up with who and how we remember, who and how we mourn, and how we dream forward. John Akomfrah: The Hour Of The Dog was co-curated by Michelle White, Senior Curator, The Menil Collection, and Cecilia Wichmann, BMA Curator and Department Head of Contemporary Art, with Oscar Flores-Montero, BMA Curatorial Assistant of Contemporary Art. John Akomfrah is a celebrated artist and filmmaker whose works investigate memory, post-colonialism, and the effects of time and aesthetics, and often explores the experiences of migrant diasporas globally. Akomfrah was a founding member of the influential Black Audio Film Collective (1982–1998), which started in London in 1982 with artists David Lawson and Lina Gopaul. Lawson and Gopaul remain his collaborators today, alongside Ashitey Akomfrah, as Smoking Dogs Films (1997–present). John Akomfrah’s work has been shown in museums and exhibitions around the world, including Smithsonian National Museum of African Art, Washington, DC; Smithsonian Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden Washington, DC; the Museum of Modern Art, New York; the New Museum, New York; Eli and Edythe Broad Art Museum, Los Angeles; Centre Pompidou, Paris; Tate, London; and the British Pavilion at the 60th Venice Biennale. Akomfrah was awarded the Artes Mundi Prize in 2017 and a Knighthood for services to the Arts in the 2023 New Year Honours. The BMA honored him in 2024 as an Artist Who Inspires.

title: Photography from The Menil Collection: Curated by Wendy Watriss
summary: Photography from The Menil Collection: Curated by Wendy Watriss is a presentation of documentary-style photographs that underscore how images can ignite conversation about diverse social realities. The exhibition features work by Larry Burrows, Henri Cartier-Bresson, Bruce Davidson, Danny Lyon, and Charles Moore, among other significant practitioners in the 20th century who explored varied approaches to capturing everyday moments, from the mundane to the monumental. The photographs on display were selected by Houston-based photographer and award-winning photojournalist Wendy Watriss. With her late husband, photographer Fred Baldwin, Watriss cofounded FotoFest, a contemporary arts organization whose biennial, city-wide celebration of international photography, established in 1986, transformed Houston’s cultural landscape, globally elevating the medium’s significance. Photography from The Menil Collection: Curated by Wendy Watriss is presented in celebration of the 40th anniversary of the Fotofest biennial in 2026. Wendy Watriss is an esteemed Houston-based photographer, curator, and photojournalist. She was the first woman to win the World Press Feature Award and the Leica Oskar Barnack Award, for her 1982 photo essay on Agent Orange published in Life. In the late 1960s, Watriss began her career as a freelance photographer and writer for publications like Newsweek and the New York Times. With her late husband, photographer Fred Baldwin, she co-founded FotoFest. In 1986 the organization hosted its first biyearly city-wide celebration of international photography and transformed Houston’s cultural landscape, elevating the medium’s significance globally. Watriss served as the Artistic Director of FotoFest for 26 years, curating and organizing more than sixty international and US exhibitions. title: The Gift of Drawing: Cy Twombly
summary: This presentation featured 27 works from a gift to the museum by the Cy Twombly Foundation. The works highlighted in the exhibition covered 30 years of the artist’s activity, from the 1950s to the 1980s and featured a broad range of materials, from graphite to oil paint; techniques such as drawing and collage; and themes that are fundamental to his entire practice, such as classical antiquity, eroticism, and nature. The works in this show, a number of which were on view for the first time, included a series of abstract landscapes from the 1980s, two untitled works from 1970 that resemble the artist’s “blackboard paintings” on view at the Cy Twombly Gallery, and Narcissus, 1975, a collage of paper, with oil, charcoal, and wax crayon on paper with the title of the work written in large capital letters across the bottom. The Gift of Drawing: Cy Twombly was curated by Edouard Kopp, John R. Eckel, Jr. Foundation Chief Curator, Menil Drawing Institute. A selection of works gifted to the museum by the Cy Twombly Foundation will open at the Menil Drawing Institute on March 27, 2026

title: Wall Drawing Series: Gladys Nilsson
summary: Gladys Nilsson’s site-specific work titled Drawing presented fantastical, hybrid beings all surrounding one monumental figure engaged in the act of drawing. A complex, garland-like arrangement of black-and-white characters soared overhead, entangled with one another, while the bystanders below, set apart by gentle color-toning, observed the scene. The bustling composition was marked by deft and fluid lines using a candy-colored palette of crayon, graphite, and acrylic paint and marker pens. Nilsson’s whimsical creation embodied her distinctive sense of humor and levity while taking viewers on a journey through the peculiar beauty of the human experience. Everything I’m interested in looking at usually involves the figure in one way or another. I’m always collecting interactions between folks that occur in daily life, and these filter into my work. The title of the piece is simply ‘Drawing.’ The idea is that the main figure is contained in this space, creating these figures, which take a life of their own. Born in Chicago in 1940, Gladys Nilsson studied painting at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago. Since 1966, Nilsson’s work has been the subject of over 50 solo exhibitions, including sixteen at Phyllis Kind Gallery (1970–1979, 1981–1983, 1987, 1991, and 1994, Chicago and New York), and two at The Candy Store (1971 and 1987, Folsom, California). Her work also has been featured in many important museum exhibitions, such as: Human Concern/Personal Torment (1969, Whitney Museum of American Art); Who Chicago? (1981, Camden Art Center, London); Parallel Visions: Modern Artists and Outsider Art (1992, Los Angeles County Museum of Art); Chicago Imagists (2011, Madison Museum of Contemporary Art, Wisconsin); and What Nerve! Alternative Figures in American Art, 1960 to the Present (2014, Museum of Art, Rhode Island School of Design, Providence).
